extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP scholars, policymakers, and advanced law students analyzing AIA prior-user rights and best-mode changes
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and interpretive guidance on the America Invents Act’s prior-user-rights provisions (§273) and the repeal of best-mode as a basis for invalidity/enforceability (§282/§15). Focuses on who may assert the defense, its limits, exceptions, and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "site" for establishing prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: A site is a factory site or other major facility in which an enterprise or line of business has made a significant capital investment, and does not include, for example, offsite locations for development of software components or manufacture of parts or ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the term "site" implies substantial capital investment; excludes incidental or offsite development/manufacture locations (example: offsite software component development or parts manufacture). (See accompanying footnote references to committee reports.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may assert the prior-user defense (person who established use vs. directed performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA law limited the defense to the person who had established the prior use (absent transfer of the entire enterprise). The AIA permits the defense to be asserted by a person who "directed the performance" of the commercial use establishing the defense (as opposed to the broader "caused" formulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history (Senator Kyl) indicates "directed" requires evidence that the defendant affirmatively instructed the vendor/contractor in the manner of the work/use; it excludes uses by vendors made without instruction or contemporaneous knowledge. Shows evolution from earlier drafts that used "caused."

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion by entities in control relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA expanded access to the prior-user defense by allowing it to be asserted by "an entity that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with" the prior user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extension permits affiliated corporate entities within control chains to invoke the defense. Cited to AIA §273(e)(1)(A) and legislative commentary noting the phrase is used across federal statutes and defined in Black’s Law Dictionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-derivation requirement (§273(e)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may not assert a defense under this section if the subject matter on which the defense is based was derived from the patentee or persons in privity with the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history indicates a rebuttable presumption of derivation if the patentee can show the prior user had access to the patentee’s information; the prior user must show independent acquisition from a non-patentee source to rebut. The Advisory Commission recommended the activity be done in good faith and without derivation. Clarifies that non-derivation is not identical to independent invention — legitimately obtaining subject matter from a third party can be non-derivative even if not independently invented by the prior user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-user rights are personal and generally non-transferable (except with business part exploiting the right)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior user rights should be personal in nature and should not be transferable, except with that part of the business which exploits the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to prevent the personal right from resembling a compulsory license-like authority; this principle appears in advisory reports and legislative commentary. Transferability is constrained to transfers of the portion of the enterprise that exploits the right (to avoid broad assignment of the personal right).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not a general license — scope limited to specific subject matter (§273(e)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The defense is not a general license under all claims of the patent at issue, but extends only to the specific subject matter for which it has been established that a qualifying commercial use occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory clause restates the "subject matter" limit and explains that "subject matter" has a relatively narrow meaning in patent law (does not include obvious variants). Legislative history and commentary emphasize that, except for the two enumerated exceptions (volume/quantity variations and certain improvements), the defense is limited to the embodiments/subject matter actually commercially used and established before the relevant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to the subject-matter limit — variations in quantity/volume and permissible improvements (§273(e)(3) exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defense shall extend to variations in the quantity or volume of use of the claimed subject matter, and to improvements in the claimed subject matter that do not infringe additional specifically claimed subject matter of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First exception ensures defendants may reasonably expand volume to meet market demand (unlike other jurisdictions that limit to prior activity levels). Second exception permits changes in the nature of use so long as the change would not infringe additional claims; illustrative example given (heating at different temperatures and claim scope). Committee report guidance: if alteration after filing would infringe claims other than those previously identified, liability follows for those additional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment of commercial use (§273(e)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who has abandoned commercial use (that qualifies under this section) of subject matter may not rely on activities performed before the date of such abandonment in establishing a defense under this section with respect to actions taken on or after the date of such abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history clarifies that abandonment does not necessarily require continuous use; seasonal or periodic uses may still qualify and not be considered abandonment if consistent with the nature of the subject matter (Senators Blunt and Kyl remarks; witness testimony about seasonal/cyclical activities). There must be no positive corroborating evidence of abandonment to permit intermittent use to survive the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: University exception to prior-user defense (§273(e)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person commercially using subject matter may not assert the defense if the claimed invention was, at the time the invention was made, owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to an institution of higher education or to a technology transfer organization whose primary purpose is commercialization of university-developed technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exception (subparagraph B) allows assertion if the activities required to reduce the invention to practice could not have been undertaken using federal funds. The incorporated definition of "institution of higher education" limits the protection to public or nonprofit accredited U.S. institutions; for-profit, unaccredited, and foreign universities remain subject to prior-user defenses. Legislative history notes the exception is not limited to patents still owned by universities — ownership at the time of invention suffices, even if the patent was later sold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity limited — §273(g) (patent not invalid under §§102/103 solely because defense exists)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall not be deemed to be invalid under section 102 or 103 solely because a defense is raised or established under this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to prevent a successful prior-user defense from automatically rendering the patent invalid under §§102/103 or making the prior user an "earlier inventor" for invalidity purposes. Legislative history notes evidence used to establish a prior-user defense could still be used separately to prove invalidity under 102/103, but establishment of §273 defense alone does not make the patent invalid. The provision harmonizes rights of later patentees and earlier commercial users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of best-mode as a basis for invalidity/enforceability (35 U.S.C. §282 amendment / AIA §15)
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure to disclose the best mode shall not be a basis on which any claim of a patent may be canceled or held invalid or otherwise unenforceable, though the best-mode requirement itself remains in 35 U.S.C. §112 as a disclosure requirement for obtaining a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIA removes best-mode as a litigation/post-grant ground for invalidity or unenforceability (and amends priority rules in §§119/120 to prevent denial of benefits based on best-mode failure). The best-mode requirement remains an examiner-reviewable application requirement under §112; once an examiner is satisfied the requirement is met, best-mode cannot later be used to challenge the patent. Legislative history justifies the change by citing the subjectivity and litigation burden of best-mode disputes; §15(c) makes the change applicable to all "proceedings" commenced after enactment (including post-grant review).
